attribution.note: Marcus wrote this sentence in his own Substack post, in his own voice.

semantics.note: The draft uses an unqualified 'will', but the sentence sits in a chain introduced by 'The likely outcome here?', so it inherits a probability hedge. The causal link to GenAI cheating comes from the context and is fine. The draft drops the hedge.

contract.note: The contract carries the 'likely outcome' qualifier over to the employer sentence, which is a fair reading of the context. It also correctly declines to invent a deadline, an employer population, or a measure for 'struggle' or 'well-educated'.

evidence.note: NACE spring 2026 survey: employers rate new grads as largely prepared, with weaker critical thinking and communication. It does not measure the effects of cheating and cannot score a hedged, undated claim.

WGU-sponsored survey of hiring professionals, published Sept 2026: 60% say AI makes candidates' skills harder to evaluate. That concerns verifying skills, not graduates' education being reduced by cheating.

reviews.rationale: The sentence continues the 'likely outcome' scenario, so under policy it is a probabilistic claim and is not scored. It also has no deadline, no defined employer population, and no measure. Both evidence items are relevant context only.
